title: Sidney Bechet on soprano and clarinet
summary: Braud praises Bechet's soprano and clarinet, his one-man-band record, and compares him to Bigard and Jimmy Noone.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Sidney Bechet: the man, the horn, the legend

blocks.x: I'm going to ask some more about that other first band we were talking about. When you had Bache and Lawrence Dewey both, did they both play clarinet or did Bache use the soprano sound?

No. Bache were playing clarinet at the time. And one of the best clarinet players ever left New Orleans or anybody's place. Because he, still today, I just heard him in Paris and I'm telling you, he's Mr. Paris. But he played the soprano. And right today, he played better clarinet than the average clarinet player. But he devoted his time with the soprano. He took up the soprano in 1918. And he wanted to play soprano. He played anything with a reed on it. He played. And he, the first fellow I heard, made a one band record. I guess you heard it, Mr. Russell.
The chic Arabian. He played trumpet. He played bass. He played piano. He played drums. He played trombone. And clarinet, himself.
When you used the two clarinets, did they play in harmony? Or did Cape Turnabout have any solos? Or one band record.

He played a plagata to what Lawrence Dewey played. And sometime, he played the top. He played the lead. And he could play a plagata. Well, that comes from natural ability. Man, just real artists. You know what I mean? And for, for singer, well, he's the best in the world. He's the best in the world. And the next best I heard for singer since, including Basset, was Biggar. And, Bonnie Biggar with Louis Armstrong, played more clarinet. Obligata and filling in than anybody I know outside of Sidney Basset. Because he had the soul. And also, Jimmy Newman. Jimmy Newman was an outstanding clarinet. Yeah, I heard that.
The tone of the biggest is room. Very fine. Very fine artists.
